title: Adaptive-Servo Admission & Kernel-Ranking for Tail-Resilient Continuous Batching
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: We see intermittent 95/99th token latency spikes during mixed short/long request workloads. Investigation points to poor admission decisions when kernel latencies vary with sequence length and attention tiling, and when prefill/decode scheduling causes decode bursts that force kernel switches mid-batch. These spikes degrade SLA for tail-sensitive customers and increase percentiles despite good median throughput.

Goal: Implement an adaptive servo-based admission controller that ranks candidate kernels per-request, shapes admission windows to stabilize tail quantiles, and schedules prefill/decode overlap to reduce kernel switching. Deliver measurable reductions in p95/p99 token latency while preserving or improving aggregate throughput and cost efficiency.

Approach summary:
1) Build a lightweight predictive kernel-ranker that maintains recent latency distributions per (model, seq_len_bucket, kernel_variant). Use exponential quantile estimators to predict 90/95/99 latency for the next window.
2) Use an adaptive servo control loop (servo-admission) that adjusts admission window sizes and slot reservations based on observed tail drift relative to p95 targets. The servo favors conservative admission when tail rises and relaxes when stable.
3) Add batch-shaping policy that prefers intra-batch kernel homogeneity: when a dominant kernel variant is predicted for incoming requests, prioritize grouping to avoid mid-batch kernel switches.
4) Modify prefill/decode scheduler to permit controlled overlap (prefill-decode pipelining) when kernel changes would otherwise trigger stalls; include per-tenant backpressure to maintain isolation.
5) Provide observability: new runtime metrics (predicted_kernel, admission_window_ms, servo_error, kernel_switch_rate) and a dashboard with token-latency heatmaps per seq_len.

Trade-offs:
- More conservative admission reduces throughput under some mixes; tune via safety knobs per-customer.
- Kernel-ranking adds a small CPU cost and memory for estimators; expected <1% host CPU.
- Prefill/decode overlap increases complexity for KV cache lifecycle; must validate memory safety.

Success metrics (targets):
- p95 token latency down by >=20% for mixed short/long workloads vs baseline (current runtime-1.22).
- p99 token latency down by >=15% for priority customers.
- No more than 3% reduction in aggregate tokens/sec across representative workloads.
- Kernel switch rate within a batch reduced by >=30% for observed mixes.

Notes: This ticket focuses on admission and scheduling logic; kernel micro-optimizations (tiling, fused attention kernels) will be tracked in separate follow-ups but the kernel-ranker should be designed to ingest kernel capability metadata (latency, switch_cost, memory_headroom).
acceptance_criteria: Servo admission loop deployed behind a feature flag; metrics emitted and visible in dashboard
p95 and p99 improvements meet targets on internal mixed-workload benchmark suite
No regressions in median latency and throughput beyond agreed thresholds
Automated canary rollout with per-route toggles and rollback on tail increase
Documentation for knobs (servo aggressiveness, max_window_ms, homogeneity threshold) in Confluence
implementation_notes: Estimator: use EWMA-based quantile estimator with decay tuned for 30s half-life
Admission loop runs in runtime control-plane thread at 50ms tick; admission decisions are stamped on requests
Kernel metadata schema: {variant, expected_tail_ms, switch_cost_ms, memory_headroom} (stored in small in-memory cache)
Batch shaping: group by predicted_kernel when homogeneity_score > 0.7; otherwise fall back to throughput-first policy
Prefill/Decode pipelining: allow decode to start on subset of slots if remaining prefills can be matched to same kernel; ensure KV cache lifetimes extended atomically
risks: Over-fitting to synthetic benchmarks: we'll validate with production traces and load tests
State explosion from too many seq_len buckets: start coarse-grained buckets and refine
Edge case: sudden large request with unknown kernel profile may be mispredicted; include safe fallback to conservative admission
Memory leak risk around extended KV cache lifetimes during overlap — require stress test
